summary: When Greeks ask to see Him, Jesus announces that His hour has come, speaks of the grain that must die, and is answered by a voice from heaven.
key_insight: The Greeks never appear again in the story. Jesus answers their request by speaking of His death: “unless a grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone.” The nations would see Him, but through the cross: “I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all peoples to Myself.”
story: Among those who came up to worship at the feast were some Greeks. They came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida of Galilee, and said, “Sir, we wish to see Jesus.” Philip told Andrew, and together they told Jesus.

Jesus answered, “The hour has come that the Son of Man should be glorified. Most assuredly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it produces much grain.” Whoever loves his life will lose it, and whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life. “If anyone serves Me, let him follow Me; and where I am, there My servant will be also.” The Father would honor anyone who served Him.

“Now My soul is troubled, and what shall I say? ‘Father, save Me from this hour’? But for this purpose I came to this hour. Father, glorify Your name.” A voice came from heaven: “I have both glorified it and will glorify it again.” Some in the crowd said it had thundered; others said an angel had spoken to Him. Jesus told them the voice had come for their sake, not His.

“Now is the judgment of this world; now the ruler of this world will be cast out. And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all peoples to Myself.” He said this to show by what death He would die. The crowd objected that the Law said the Christ remains forever. “Who is this Son of Man?” they asked. Jesus warned them that the light would be with them only a little while longer. “While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become sons of light.” Then He went away and hid Himself from them.

Though He had done so many signs before them, they did not believe in Him. Isaiah had foreseen it: “Lord, who has believed our report?” Isaiah said these things when he saw His glory and spoke of Him. Even so, many of the rulers believed in Him, but they would not confess it for fear of being put out of the synagogue, “for they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God.”

Jesus cried out, “He who believes in Me, believes not in Me but in Him who sent Me. And he who sees Me sees Him who sent Me. I have come as a light into the world, that whoever believes in Me should not abide in darkness.” He had not come to judge the world but to save it. Yet the word He had spoken would judge whoever rejected Him on the last day, for He spoke only what the Father had commanded, “and I know that His command is everlasting life.”

scene.label: Greeks at the feast
scene.text: These were Gentiles, not Greek-speaking Jews. They had come up “to worship,” so they were probably God-fearers drawn to Israel’s God, like the Ethiopian official (Acts 8:27). They were welcome in the temple’s outer court but barred from the inner courts, so even their request had to pass through others.

scene.label: Philip and Andrew
scene.text: Both had Greek names, and both came from Bethsaida (John 1:44), near the largely Gentile lands east of the Jordan. That may be why the Greeks approached Philip. Andrew is the disciple who keeps bringing people to Jesus (1:41–42; 6:8–9).

scene.label: “Lifted up”
scene.text: John uses this phrase three times for the cross (3:14; 8:28; 12:32). It echoes Isaiah’s suffering Servant, who “shall be exalted and extolled and be very high” (Isaiah 52:13). In John, the cross is both execution and exaltation.

scene.label: “The Christ remains forever”
scene.text: The crowd had promises in mind such as Psalm 89:36 and Isaiah 9:7, which say the Messiah’s throne will last forever. A Messiah who would be lifted up to die did not fit what they expected.

scene.label: Isaiah saw His glory
scene.text: John quotes Isaiah 53:1 and Isaiah 6:10, then says Isaiah spoke “when he saw His glory.” In Isaiah 6 the prophet saw the Lord “high and lifted up” on His throne. John says the glory Isaiah saw was the glory of Jesus.

witnesses.john: Only John records this scene, and with it he closes Jesus’ public ministry; chapters 13–17 belong to the disciples alone. John adds his own reflection on Israel’s unbelief from Isaiah, and ends with Jesus’ cry that believing in Him is believing in the One who sent Him. John alone gives the prayer “Now My soul is troubled,” and he does not record the agony in Gethsemane that the other Gospels describe.

seeing.reveals: Jesus faces His death with open eyes and a troubled soul, and still chooses it: “for this purpose I came to this hour.” He sees the cross as His glory and the means by which He will draw people of every nation to Himself.
seeing.living: The Greeks asked to see Jesus, and He pointed them to a seed falling into the ground. Following Him means walking the same road: letting go of the life you would cling to, so that it can bear fruit for others. And He promises that where He is, His servant will be also.
seeing.ponder: What are you holding so tightly that it remains alone, when Jesus is calling you to let it fall into the ground?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus is glorified through death, and those who follow Him find life the same way.
outline: A request that signals the hour (20–23)
The cross that draws all peoples (31–33)
preaching.watch_for: Again and again in John, Jesus’ hour had “not yet come” (2:4; 7:30; 8:20). When Gentiles come asking for Him, He says, “The hour has come” (12:23). From here every step leads to the cross.
